svg.aria-label: Diagram: where tenant isolation actually lives in a pooled AWS architecture, across a shared table and a shared queue. On the left, the shared DynamoDB table: the partition key is the isolation boundary, and every partition is designed to deliver a maximum of 3,000 read units per second and 1,000 write units per second, so if the tenant identifier is the partition key that figure is a per-tenant ceiling that provisioning more table capacity does not raise. The ceiling is expressed in units rather than operations, so item size consumes it: AWS's worked example shows a 20 KB item costing 5 read units per consistent read, leaving 600 consistent reads per second against that single item before the partition limit is reached. On the right, the shared SQS queue: the queue has no notion of a tenant unless the producer sets a MessageGroupId, which fair queues use as the tenant identifier. Amazon SQS detects a noisy neighbour by monitoring how in-flight messages are distributed among tenants, and when one tenant holds a disproportionate share it prioritises delivery for the others, protecting their dwell time. A panel records what the mitigation does not do: Amazon SQS does not limit the consumption rate per tenant, so this is prioritisation rather than throttling, and consumers still receive noisy-tenant messages when capacity is free. A second panel records the trap: MessageGroupId does not mean the same thing on a standard queue as on a FIFO queue, where on standard queues it is only a tenant identifier and does not enforce ordering, so the same producer field changes meaning entirely with the queue type it is sent to.
svg.title: Two shared resources, two tenant identifiers, both chosen upstream
svg.text: Nobody chose the isolation model. Two fields did.
In a pooled design, the boundary is whatever the shared resource uses to tell tenants apart.
Shared table — the boundary is the partition key
Every partition is designed to deliver at most
3,000 read units/s · 1,000 write units/s
If the tenant id is the partition key, that is a
per-tenant ceiling. Table capacity does not raise it.
And it is spent in units, not operations:
20 KB item → 5 read units per read
→ 600 reads/s, not 3,000
A schema that grows its rows lowers every tenant's ceiling.
Shared queue — the boundary is a producer field
The queue knows nothing of tenants until:
MessageGroupId = “tenant-123”
SQS watches how in-flight messages are shared out.
One tenant holding a disproportionate share is noisy;
SQS then prioritises delivery for everyone else.
Noisy by volume or by cost — a tenant whose
messages simply take longer to process counts too.
No consumer change. No API latency cost. No throughput limit.
What fairness is not
“Amazon SQS does not limit the consumption
rate per tenant.”
Prioritisation, not a quota. It changes who waits.
The same field, two meanings
On FIFO, MessageGroupId enforces ordering.
On standard it is “only a tenant identifier and
does not enforce message ordering.”
Alarm on the quiet groups, not the queue
Queue-level depth and age both move when one tenant surges. ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisibleInQuietGroups
reports the rest — the difference between the two lines is the whole diagnosis.
Neither boundary looks like an isolation decision when it is made. One is a data-modelling choice; the other is a line that looks like metadata.
Both are cheap on the day they are written, and a migration on every day after.
